year if he tries to collect licence fees in our section of the country, if we do not get better service than we get at the present time. Dozens of people have been brought before the police magistrates because they refused to pay the $2 licence fee; they claim, and rightly, that they should not pay because they are not getting the service. In the past it has been held that people who are taxed should be represented, and in connection with radio, whether under private or government control, if they do not get the service they should not be expected to pay the fees. Many of the people are refusing to pay again this year, for the reasons I have already given.
It is not my intention to take up very much of the time of the committee in this connection, because the Minister of Marine must be fully seized of this situation. We do not place the blame at the door of the commission; we place it entirely on the shoulders of the government, because surely during the last three years they have had time to study the situation. When the nationalization of radio was first mentioned we were unanimous in our support in northern Ontario. Perhaps we were a bit selfish; under private ownership we were not getting the reception that was given in the cities. To our sorrow, however, we found that though we were expected to contribute $2 per year for a licence fee, we were not receiving the service we had expected, while under private ownership at least we did not have to pay the licence fee. If under private ownership we did not get the programs we expected we had only ourselves to blame for buying radios, and we had no fees to pay. Surely the government must be seized of the situation; surely the pioneer population of northern Ontario and northern Quebec should receive the same consideration as is shown the rest of the country. Is this the case because there are only one or two members interested in the question? Would it be any different if there were a dozen or two dozen members giving voice to the sentiments of those people? I claim always to have been fair in discussing public matters and questions affecting my section of the country. I know the hon. member for Pontiac (Mr. Belec), who sits opposite, is absolutely with me in this regard, and I am positive that the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gordon) is also with me, because in Haileybury and the rest of his constituency the people are not getting the radio reception to which they are entitled.
I should like to read some brief articles coming from my own part of the country in order that the committee may be fully

aware of the exact situation. The first is from the Northland Post of Cochrane, under date of April 111, 1935:
The radio situation in the north remains in the same unsatisfactory condition. Repeated protests on the part of every paper in the north, and efforts on the part of our local member, Mr. Bradette, have so far failed to produce any tangible results. It is time that the radio commission either put up or shut up, in the popular language of the day. Either an honest effort should be made to give satisfactory service, or else the government should exempt radio users in the north from the payment of the annual licence fee. It is neither just nor reasonable to expect the radio users in the north to pay an annual fee to the Canadian government, which is used to furnish programs to certain other sections of the country, when all that we in the north can get satisfactorily are American stations.
This is right to the point, and from a paper in my section of the country. I shall now read to the committee a resolution passed by the New Liskeard board of trade, New Liskeard, Ontario, a point in the constituency of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gordon).	This
letter addressed to the Minister of Labour, the radio commission and to myself is as follows:
New Liskeard, Ont., April 3, 1935. Mr. J. A. Bradette, M.P.,
Parliament Buildings,
Ottawa, Ontario.
Dear Sir:
At the annual meeting of the New Liskeard board of trade held on January 31st, the following resolution re a broadcasting station for northern Ontario was passed:
"That the proposed resolution before the Associated Boards of Trade be followed up. This resolution reads as follows:	'That the
dominion government, through the radio commission be requested to establis a radio broadcasting station at some suitable point north of North Bay or Sudbury of such a capacity as will eliminate present interference and give the radio users of northern Ontario and northwestern Quebec the service which is being received by radio owners in old Ontario.'"
Since then other representations to the commission have been made and at a meeting of the executive of the New Liskeard board of trade held on April 1st, the following resolution pertaining to a radio station in the north was passed:	.
"That the secretary write to the Canadian radio broadcasting commission, Hon. W. A. Gordon. Mr. J. A. Bradette, associated boards of trade and the town council, repeating the motion already placed on the books and conveying to them the information that regardless of representations conveyed to them otherwise, we still maintain that only a broadcasting station of the type described in our motion will satisfy the situation."

Would the hon.
member permit a word? As we are anxious to put through some further legislation before the adjournment which will take place tomorrow, may I tell the hon. member that to-

Radio Broadcasting
day I am issuing a licence to Kirkland Lake station increasing the power from 100 watts to 1,000 watts, and placing that station on the wave length 530. It is the view of the commission that for the time being this change will give a satisfactory service to northern Ontario. Something better may be done later on, but in the meantime we expect the change will give fairly good service. I make this statement to the hon. member in order to curtail the debate.

I wish to oblige the
minister in every possible way, because I believe the radio commission and his department are anxious to help my section of the country. I must say however that a 1,000 watt station at Kirkland Lake is not going to remedy the situation. The only redeeming feature in the statement made by the minister is the fact that in the near future something might be done. "Might be done" will not satisfy us, either. For the last three years we have been suffering through lack of service. We have paid the government thousands of dollars for services to which we are entitled. As I said a few moments ago, and as was stated by the hon. member who preceded me, I have no quarrel with the private stations. But surely the government does not expect those private stations to give the service the people may expect. I cannot accept a 1,000 watt station at Kirkland Lake under private jurisdiction, as a permanent solution of the problem. I have no quarrel with the private owners; as a matter of fact the owner of that station is a personal friend of mine. I do say however that this state of affairs cannot remain. May I put this question to the minister? Is it true that during the course of this winter it was the intention of his department to increase the power of a station in Toronto to a point where it would give service to my section of the country, or is it true that the government intended installing a heavy relay station in northern Ontario?

Mr. Chairman, I
know the radio commission has before it a program which will implement the report of the committee, and will provide for the installation of a' certain number of powerful stations throughout Canada. My recollection is that a station is contemplated for northern Ontario. To answer the hon. member and the hon. member for North Waterloo, however, I must say that we are faced with the matter of expenditures. Until now, under the terms of the act, the radio commission can meet the expenses only through the revenues derived from licence fees. When they have met the expenses in connection with programs 92582-177
wires and so on, there is not very much left for capital expenditure and for the installation of powerful stations. It is only a matter of expenditure. Although we have had this program before us for some time, I did not think it advisable to authorize action, in view of the discussion which is to take place after the recess concerning the future life of the radio commission, as it now exists under the law.
I think the hon. member should be satisfied with the licence I am issuing to-day at Kirkland Lake. If my hon. friend will state positively that my action will not ameliorate the situation, I am quite content to suspend the order for this licence.
Hear, hear.

The radio commissioners contend the proposed station will ameliorate the situation, but if the hon. member will take the responsibility, as a representative from that part of the country, to state that what we propose to do would not in any way, shape or form ameliorate the situation, then I am quite content to leave the station at 100 watts, as it has been for the past few years.

Of course, I do not
believe the minister has the right to make me responsible for such a decision. There is no doubt that the increased power at Kirkland Lake will improve the situation and will improve the reception. I accept it, however, only on one condition-and I am speaking for the people in my section of the country- that the proposed action will be considered as only temporary.
I believe we are practical and logical in our representations. A few moments ago the minister stated that in the near future something tangible would be given to us. Surely his department will not say that a 1,000 watt station at Kirkland Lake would be sufficient for the great area of northern Ontario and northern Quebec. It would be physically impossible for that station to be sufficient. Surely the minister does not say that such a station would give service to the towns of Cochrane, Kapuskasing, Hearst, Timmins, Iroquois Falls, or to other sections of northern Quebec. I will accept the suggestion as a temporary measure but not as a solution. I appreciate what the minister has said, and appreciate his activity. I must urge, however, that what he is doing must be considered only a palliative, and we hope the government may find it possible to give us a strong relay station, a short wave station, or some facilities by which we may receive properly

Radio Broadcasting

the programs from the Canadian commission.
Surely the people in the northern sections must be classed as Canadians and as such are entitled to Canadian programs. At the present time we are getting programs from Mexico, the United States; even the programs from old England, come in more clearly than do the programs of the Canadian radio commission. I know the minister wishes to be fair, and I make my plea to him sincerely and earnestly. In that northern section of Canada we have a quarter of a million people who have done yeoman work in the development of Canada but who, when they turn the dials of their radios, cannot get the programs of Canadian stations. Surely the minister does not wish that condition to exist. I would gladly accept this little station-and I emphasize the word "little"-which will give only a limited service to a very limited area, on the condition that something further may be done. It would not give sendee to the population I have just mentioned. I should like the minister to tell me, if it is possible for him to. do so, and if he can do so the people in the district will be very thankful, whether we shall before the next one or two years be given the same sort of service that is given in other parts of Canada.

My hon. friend understands the difficulties of the situation. It is admitted by everyone that it is a very difficult district to serve. If ever there was a case where it is proven that there is no political influence in this matter it is ini this one, because the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gordon) has been working in conjunction with my hon. friend in order to secure a better service for that district. I know that my hon. friend understands the difficulties of the situation. For the time being we are trying to give some measure of satisfaction, and later on we shall strive to give a better service.

Would the minister enlarge on that "later on"? We know when a bill is coming due, but the minister's "later on" is too indefinite, and if we have to wait for years for a better service that would be far too long for us to accept and would be absolutely unfair to our people.

I want to make a few
remarks in defence of the Windsor station which my hon. friend from North Waterloo (Mr. Euler), who I am sorry is not in his seat, criticizes every year, owing to the fact that his friends did not get the licence that was promised to them before the late government went out of power.
iMr. Bradette.]
I have no brief for the radio commission, but I want to tell my hon. friend that a licence was granted to the Essex broadcasting station before the radio commission was established. There were two 5,000 watt stations in western Ontario. Now there is one, and there is a 100 watt station at London and a radio commission station. The Windsor station is one of the finest stations on the North American continent; the residents of Ottawa and the residents of the Soo got their best reception from this station. It is not the fault of the Windsor station that their wavelength has been changed three times. First it was 540, which was satisfactory, then it was changed to 840, which was satisfactory, and then it was changed to 1030, which has brought all sorts of confusion.
My hon. friend from North Waterloo said that this station was owned and controlled by the Columbia broadcasting system of the United States. I may tell him that Canadians hold the majority stock in that station, and only within the last few days the Columbia Broadcasting system has cancelled its contract with the Windsor station owing to the poor reception on the new wave length 1030. Before that station was established we were unable in the border cities and in that neck of the woods to get any radio at all except what came through Detroit or Cleveland or some other American station. For some reason or other we cannot get the Toronto or London or Chatham stations. That is an established fact which cannot be disputed.
My hon. friend from North Waterloo was very severe in his criticism and said that there should be an investigation of that station. He insinuated that a scandal would be discovered. I do not know what he wants to investigate, and I am quite sure that the station would welcome an investigation. I do not know what grounds my hon. friend has for making that statement, but whoever gave him his information evidently had not the facts before him. I think I have covered the situation as to the Windsor station, Mr. Chairman. The station there has cost over $150,000 a year and is employing about thirty people. It has been a benefit to our section of the country, and I do not think anyone has any just criticism to make of it.

I have listened to the
remarks of the hon. members for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) and West Essex (Mr. Robinson) on the question of radio broadcasting in this dominion. I am not unmindful of the tremendous educational facilities that

Radio Broadcasting
are at the disposal of the Canadian radio broadcasting commission, and, notwithstanding the remarks of the last speaker, I have no sympathy with the attitude and the policy of the broadcasting station in the city of Windsor. I think it is a fair observation to make, notwithstanding any opinion to the contrary, that it reflected the broadcasting policy of one of the great American chains, and while that policy may have been changed in the last week or two it has been generally understood that that Windsor station was more or less in the Columbia broadcasting chain.
Entirely.

Entirely, if you will. I am prepared to go that distance, and it was because of the lack of channels that existed in the country to the south of us. When the Canadian radio broadcasting commission was set in motion there was the driving force of the unanimous opinion of members of this House of Commons behind it for the purpose of reflecting the viewpoint of the Canadian people. We wanted a system developed that would reflect the viewpoint of the people of this dominion. Taking into consideration the limited vision of the average member of this House of Commons, the purpose was the inculcation of the basic philosophy of the Canadian people, expressed in the message carried over the air by the Canadian radio broadcasting commission. Recently the Prime Minister made a number of speeches over the Canadian radio commission system, and I have no quarrel with that. Nor have I any criticism to offer of the opinions expressed by the Prime Minister. Being a labour man, believing in a democracy, and having a very fixed opinion that the progress of civilization has been in proportion to the freedom of its institutions, I say I have no quarrel with a policy that permitted the Prime Minister, because of his financial ability to use the facilities of the Canadian radio commission, to broadcast his message to the people of Canada. I only wish that the leader of the opposition could do the same thing, and that the leader of the polyglot Cooperative Commonwealth Federation could also do the same; but that opportunity should not be predicated upon their financial ability to use the facilities of the Canadian radio commission. I think that that financial obligation should rest upon the people of Canada. I think that the leader of the government, the leader of the opposition. and the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation, and incidentally the leader of the Labour party, which is myself at the moment because I am the only one 92582-1771
left here, should be free to enunciate their philosophy to the people through the instrumentality of the Canadian radio broadcasting commission without incurring the disability of the financial obligations that go with it.
Let me say this very frankly-and it is just as well that I should say it because it is my opinion. I still think that there are a number of points of view which we are obliged to take into consideration. There are for instance the points of view of the two major political parties. There is the view of those who feel that they reflect the opinion of the farmers and again there are members of the House of Commons who have not reached the stage where they are ashamed to call themselves labour men. I do not want to say anything in the spirit of criticism, because after all the right to differ is the driving force of our civilization; indeed, it is the greatest contribution which the Anglo-Saxon race has made to the science of government throughout the history of the world. That contribution is the right of men to hold different views even though they may call one another names in passing. I have passed through the last four years in this House of Commons and, so far as I am concerned, the reduction in wages and salaries of civil servants is something that I opposed from the first, whereas some members of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation took exactly the opposite position. Well, I have no quarrel with them on that score, but there you have a fundamental difference in this so-called political party which is supposed to reflect the new Utopia that will exist in this country. I have no quarrel with my good friends the farmers. They have been under the tremendous pressure of a fall in the price level in this and every other country and naturally they felt that if the farmers had to suffer a reduction in their remuneration, as indicated by that decline in price levels, other people should do the same. I took the opposite view; I regretted that anyone should have thrown sand into the machinery. In this regard I want to pay my compliments to the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough (Mr. Duff), who supported me in that argument. I have always held the view that if low wages were an essential part of any government policy then the only thing for the people to do would be to emulate the Chinese and the people of India and walk around in their bare skins, and we should all be rich. Again, with respect to the hours of labour, it has not been possible in this comer to get sufficient votes to reflect the point of view of the Canadian people
Radio Broadcasting

on the absolute necessity of reducing the hours to meet the problems that inevitably face this country. I do not wish to point out any fundamental weaknesses in this so-called new political party, but I do want to point out to the government that, with the power which they can exercise, it should be possible in the next election for the leaders of the respective avenues of thought in this dominion to express their views over the radio, free from the financial restrictions that otherwise hamper them. They should be able to broadcast the views of the people of Canada without being obliged to make any financial contribution to the broadcasting facilities of Canada. Radio users throughout the country are called upon to pay an annual licence fee of S2 towards the maintenance of the Canadian Radio Broadcasting Commission, but I think it would be a wise policy if the political leaders were allowed the use of the radio during an election. I have always contended that all our British institutions are predicated upon an appeal to reason rather than to prejudice, and that appeal should not be made to rest upon the financial resources of any party that desires to express its views on the floor of the house-views that are held by any section of the Canadian people. We are entering upon a general election in which various points of view will be presented to the people and it would be wise, in my opinion, to regard the speeches of the different political leaders, not from the point of view of party politics but as individual contributions to the political education of the nation. These broadcasts should be regarded as a public service, on the same footing as we treat our schools at the present time, and the philosophy of any political party should not be made dependent upon its ability to meet the financial obligations of the broadcasting system of the country. In this respect I think the authorities here might take a leaf out of the book of the National Broadcasting Company and of the Columbia Broadcasting Company in the United States and regard the speeches of our political leaders in the next election as a contribution to the political education of the people. It should not be predicated upon the ability of the respective leaders to draw upon campaign funds.

Regardless of the method of administration whch may be finally decided upon by the government in the interim between now and the time when the projected legislation is brought down, I wish to direct to the attention of the minister the situation in western Nova Scotia. As pointed out to

me, western Nova Scotia is not getting the benefit of a proper radio service. I have before me a letter which was published in the Halifax Chronicle of April 9, from a citizen of western Nova Scotia, which I understand was sent in to the department:
I have your notice that my licence fee for $2 is due. I have always been ready and willing to pay my radio licence and was in favour of dominion control of radio but the government has not given us, in the maritimes, the service it professed to tax us for. I have been -paying my tax for years but I get nothing in real program service from your department. I shall, therefore, pay my tax under protest. The radio commission's programs, especially at night are no good to us, whatever, in these maritimes. Apart from the terrific local noises that are set up we are overwhelmed by powerful stations from outside Canada or so "jammed" that there is nothing but a howl through our Canadian station.
I want to register with the minister if I can an emphatic request that something be done to improve the radio situation in the western portion of our province. I brought the matter to the attention of the chairman of the radio commission on several occasions. He has assured me that some steps of that kind are being taken, but nothing is done and the situation portrayed in the letter from which I have just quoted is confirmed by a letter which I received only yesterday from my own constituency and which intimates that they are not getting in that section the service for which they are paying. I want to point out to the minister, as I have done to the chairman of the radio commission, that the agency through which better service can be rendered to western Nova Scotia is station CJLS, established at Yarmouth considerably over a year ago, a station, as I understand from those who know, with most modern equipment, up to date, well managed by people who know their business technically and by people who are putting on excellent programs. That station could serve western Nova Scotia well. A licence was granted to it by the radio commission, but so far it has been refused arrangements whereby it can handle the Canadian commission's programs. The result is that in the evenings at a time when radio listeners want to have that service, they do not get the benefit of the good service from Halifax or Saint John, because those stations are blurred as they come in. All they get is the good and bad programs from the United States stations, and their own station, CJLS has only the local programs which are excellent but which should be supplemented by outside programs. Listeners in that section of the country are paying their fee of $2 and are not getting any value

Radio Broadcasting
for their money. The minister may expect that those citizens will protest very vigorously against continuing to pay licence fees supposedly for the purpose of keeping up a Canadian radio commission and having supplied to them Canadian commission programs when they are not getting this service because the commission declines to make the necessary arrangements to have this efficient station handle their programs. I bring this to the attention of the minister and urge upon him, as I have urged upon the chairman of the commission, a right-about face and a recognition of the rights of the citizens of Western Nova Scotia and the ability of station CJLS to serve them. I believe a local station of this kind, which is well equipped and well run, not a makeshift or cheap station in any sense, should be encouraged. The people who have established it are enterprising and capable. Apparently that portion of Nova Scotia is peculiarly situated so far as atmospheric conditions are concerned. Nobody knows less about the technical side of radio broadcasting than I but I understand that on account of geographic or atmospheric conditions it is difficult to get stations at Montreal or Toronto and after Halifax and Saint John. Therefore there is need for a local station, and I urge the minister in the interim between now and the time when the legislation is brought down, to give favourable consideration to this matter. The commission has had the strongest representations not only from station CJLS but from more than one thousand radio listeners-in who sent in a petition some time ago pointing out the deficiencies in the present service and praying that arrangements be made whereby the commission's programs be handled by that well equipped and efficient station CJLS.

From the discussion that has grown out of this bill and the various criticisms we have heard from all sides of the house, I think if anybody had any doubt as to the merits of the case and the work that has been done by the commission since its inception, he will be satisfied to-day that the commission has not lived up to expectations. If anybody had any doubt that the commission was going to remain long in existence, from the speeches that have been made to-day I think we are justified in saying that this bill which has been brought before the house sounds the death knell of the commission. I for one would not be willing to allow this bill to go through had we not had a certain kind of intimation or assurance from the government of the day that within the next month or two we are to have a new piece of
legislation, a new way of controlling this commission, which apparently has not been doing what it was created to do or develop.
I agree entirely with the remarks that have been made by the hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) and the hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler). All that they have said is quite true. So far as the part of the country from which I come is concerned, I agree also to a large extent with the remarks made by my deskmate, the hon. member for SheLbume-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston). I have had on many occasions to point out to the members of the commission the difficulty experienced by some of the people in outlying districts of my constituency of Charlevoix-Montmorency and further down along the coast in getting any station and having the advantage of certain good programs. On these occasions the answer has been that the commission would have to spend huge amounts to erect the powerful stations necessary to keep from coming into this country what was called at that time the bootlegging radio business that used to come in from the United States and Mexico.
Apparently at the present time the commission is working under certain disadvantages, and I realize that. But it was a huge undertaking, anid I do not think before this government took office anyone ever visualized the creation of such a commission that would go into the field of broadcasting operations, doing the same kind of business as some of the private institutions are doing. We have it to-day on the authority of the hon. member for North Waterloo that instead of decreasing the number of these stations and getting them coordinated, we have had the number of private stations increased from forty-nine to' fifty-nine. This all goes to prove that while the government might have been well inten-tioned at the time they started building up this commission, they have missed their aim and have not been successful in giving satisfaction to the Canadian public from coast to coast.
As to what has been said about those who were members of the commission, I think in the beginning from the point of view of our province some better choice might have been made. It was said in connection with the persons from our province who were appointed to the commission, that they were men connected with political organizations. Some have tried to say that they were not, but one gentleman was a candidate running against me in the last general election, and another, although the contrary may be stated, was assistant to the chief organizer of the author-
Radio Broadcasting

ized body of the Conservative party in Montreal when the elections were going on in that district. Although those gentlemen are amiable and apart from politics may be quite estimable, we cannot expect other than political patronage when the question of administering such a big commission as this arises. From the remarks made in the house to-day from all comers we learn-and the hon. member for North Waterloo has so stated-that there has been on many occasions quite a little bit of political patronage and advantage given this way or the other, on this side or on that, to favour certain districts against others.
Another matter that has been repeatedly pointed out to me in the city of Montreal, where I live and practise Jaw, is that in the direction of programs and also in the selection and hiring of the services of some artists, there has been in some instances discrimination. Some of them have been favoured as against others who might have had just as good or as valuable talents, but who could not get a hearing because they did not seem to be able to interview the personnel of the commission as well as others would appear to be able to do. It is pretty hard to get concrete cases in point and written documents or information as to these facts, because the persons concerned were not willing at the time to disclose the facts, being afraid that later on, should they have a chance to be employed by other companies to do broadcasting elsewhere, they would be debarred and prevented from having a chance to make a living.
Another feature which is in the mind of the people generally is that the commission has cost a great deal of money, and also that some of the expenses, such as travelling expenses of the chairman and members of the commission, have been very great and out of proportion. It has been stated to me many a time that such expensive trips were taken by the commission. I have not in mind all the places to which they went, but for instance about a year ago I understand a trip was taken by some members of the commission to Newfoundland. I would like to know what they had to do there, what they could learn there regarding better administration of radio broadcasting in Canada. Possibly we had something that Newfoundland could learn, but I do not think it was in the interests of the commission to send the members there. And I was told on good authority that those trips and excursions cost a lot of money. Before sitting down I would ask the minister, who although he disclaims being in charge of the commission is responsible for it in the house, to tell me how I could obtain,-for I should like in all sincerity to obtain it before the passage

of this bill,-a statement of all the expenses of all the commissioners each year since they have been appointed, and where they have been and the cost in detail. I think the house ought to know this. I say that because it is in the minds of the people, the country wants to know it, and the house is entitled to have an account of those expenses. I do not know if the government would like to appoint a committee by which this matter could be investigated. There was a committee last year or the year before which dealt with the organization of the commission, but I am not aware that these facts were disclosed. In order to set right complaints that have been made, before the bill passes we should have a detailed statement of the expenses of the commissioners for all their trips.

Last year when
I first approached the minister in an effort to get some information regarding the radio commission, I was ruled out of order. Then I tried to get some information as to the expenditure of the commission, and its workings, but was informed that they were not responsible to any minister or anybody and the information could not be had. Then the leader of the opposition consulted with the Prime Minister and I got some figures as to the expenses of the commission, but these figures I am not able to understand. I have also consulted several auditors and they are of the same opinion. So the hon. member who asked for a statement as to the expenditure of the commission certainly has my hearty support.
As far as British Columbia is concerned, as I was trying last year to explain to the committee, we are forced to pay two dollars for a licence, and something like seventy thousand licences were paid for last year in British Columbia. But there are hundreds of people who do not pay the licence fee, and those who are paying protest because they are unable to hear any Canadian program. I have a radio in Prince Rupert and I have one three hundred miles inland where I have my summer home, and I have been unable yet to get a Canadian radio commission program on either of them. It may be that my sets are not up to date, but I am trying to get the best there is. I understand that the minister intends to improve the station in Vancouver, and I am very glad to hear that. In my room here I have dozens of letters complaining about this radio situation in British Columbia, and especially in the outlying parts. If we are to keep on paying a licence fee to the commission we are at least entitled to have Canadian programs; if that is impossible I think we should not have to pay the licence fee. I hope that

Radio Broadcasting
when the bill is brought before the house consideration will be given to these complaints, and I plead especially for the part of the country which I represent and know something about.

In answer to the three hon. members who have spoken last, let me say that at the present time I do not intend to answer on behalf of the radio commission all the complaints and charges which have been made before this committee. To-morrow this house will adjourn, and we have important legislation which we would like to put through before to-morrow evening. At the present time we are only asking the extension of the life of the commission for two months. The questions raised to-day will be taken up again when the estimates come before the committee. We do not admit the charges made, but we do not propose to answer them now except to say that the policy of imposing a licence fee on radio owners is not our policy; it is the policy of my hon. friends. When we came into power citizens who owned radios had to pay the licence fee. As to the lack of coverage, I have already stated that the radio commission has a program of construction including a certain number of powerful stations, one in Vancouver, one in the eastern provinces, and at other places where the service is found to be poor, and it is hoped this will give entire satisfaction. But it involves expenditure, and I can state to the committee that the amount collected for radio licence fees was not sufficient to allow the commission to build powerful stations. This matter will be brought before the house after the recess; another bill will be introduced or the matter will be referred to a committee and the whole question will be debated at length to the satisfaction of my hon. friends. What we a-sk at the present time is to let the matter stand. The extension is only for two months, and ample opportunity will be given to every hon. member to satisfy his constituents when the matter comes up again after the recess.

I just want to say one
word, and I need not apologize for it. We sympathize with the minister and the government in their desire to expedite certain legislation which needs to be expedited-

In the interests of
the country.

-but it will be admitted that we are not responsible for the fact that we are going home for five weeks. I want to impress upon the government, since they are going to consider this question during the recess and there is the possibility of another
bill being introduced, to give consideration to the suggestion of my hon. friend from East Hamilton (Mr. Mitchell) that on the publicly owned stations the leaders of the various political parties in parliament should be free to speak and set forth their views to the people of 'Canada. It is all very well to say: Let them pay for it; but that places those who have not financial means at their disposal in a position of inferiority. It does not seem quite fair that these publicly owned stations, organized for the people of Canada and paid for by the taxes of all people, not only the money received through the sale of radio licences but the taxes used in the ordinary way to pay any deficits resulting from the administration of the service, should be used only by public men who can afford to pay for the privilege, of broadcasting their views to the people of Canada.

I do not want to interrupt my hon. friend; I am interested in what he is saying, but I should like him to explain on what basis he would divide the time, between how many parties and how many leaders, and in what proportion.

It cannot be more difficult here than it is in the old country. I remember discussing the matter last year with Sir Herbert Samuel at the home of my right hon. leader, and that gentleman told us what has been done in England. There they have allocated part of the time to the various political parties, not only during election campaigns but all the time. I do not know whether they speak once a week, once a fortnight or once a month, but it is being done. Sir Herbert Samuel told me, for instance, that Mr. Winston Churchill tried to claim the right to speak as well as the leaders, because he thought he was the leader of a party consisting of himself, but his claims were not recognized. There are certainly in this country three parties which are well defined; perhaps there are four or five, but those gentlemen can arrange among themselves as to who should speak for them. Perhaps the ex-Minister of Trade and Commerce would claim to be a leader, too. At any rate I think we might arrange that at least three Leaders should have the privilege of speaking over the radio.
Why not the hon. member for Temiscouata?

Possibly, and at times the hon. member for North Renfrew might qualify for a kind of leadership. The commission are paying the artists who entertain the radio listeners. Well, I think the public of Canada would enjoy listening to the
Radio Broadcasting

addresses of all the political leaders, and I am sure they would not charge anything for delivering those addresses.
The listeners would not pay anything, anyway.
And they should not be made to pay. I think perhaps some would pay to listen to my hon. friend from Lincoln, who is very interesting at times.

I should like to say just one further word, Mr. Chairman. As I have said, I am very much interested in the suggestion put forward by the hon. member for Quebec East. I am not speaking for the government at all, but in my personal view it would be a very good thing indeed if some arrangement could be made for the use of the radio at election time by the various parties. I have thought it over, however, and I cannot think of any way in which we can divide up the time and have it satisfactory to everybody. I am not unmindful of the criticism of the radio commission that has come from many quarters, but I wish to remind the committee again that their task has been exceedingly difficult. To my mind that task, however, is an easy one compared with what would be necessary if my hon. friend from Quebec East should present a plan dividing up part of the time among the various political parties. My own impression is that he would receive nothing but criticism after he finished with that arrangement.
I was greatfy interested in the remarks of my hon. friend from North Waterloo (Mr. Euler), who is always worth hearing in regard to matters of this kind. The hon. member is greatly in favour of public ownership. Many difficulties have confronted the radio commission, but I still feel personally that we ought to be able to carry on this service by a commission. How it can be done I am not at present in a position to state-
Oh, oh.

I admit that
quite frankly. There are sections of the country to which it is impossible to give good service under present conditions. To provide only five or six powerful stations, as my hon. friend suggests, would mean wiping out all these private stations, which no one would suggest unless they received some consideration.

That would not need to
follow.

Sir GEORGE PERLEY":	I suppose it
would eventually. Certainly the local difficulties in various parte of Canada are extremely hard to avoid and overcome. However, all I can say is that the purpose of this bill is simply to lengthen the life and authority of the commission for two months. The Prime Minister will be here when we meet again and in the meantime this question will be given consideration. I did not state that any new arrangement would be made, as one hon. member suggested; I simply stated that the whole matter is under careful consideration. Therefore I would ask the committee to pass this bill.

Title agreed to.

Bill No. 57 for the relief of Albertine Roberte Montpellier de Beaujeu-Mr. Bell (St. Antoine).
fMr. Laurtn.)
Mr. W. G. ERNST (Queens-Lunenburg) moved that the Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee on Bill No. 43, for the relief of Clarence MacGregor Roberts.

I think it is a matter of regret that this motion has been made, that the Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of the whole on this particular bill. This bill, as the house knows, has come to us from the senate. Tiie senate passed the bill granting the divorce. According to the usage of this house the bill came to the private bills committee of this house and that committee saw fit to report the preamble not proven. I say it is regrettable that the bill has come back to the house, and I make that statement for a number of reasons. One reason is that it is a private bill and will occupy the time of the house for an hour, thus preventing the discussion of public bills. It will hold its place on the order paper until finally disposed of. There is reason to believe that this bill will occasion a good deal of debate not only on the motion that the Speaker leave the chair but in committee of the. whole, if it should go there. I think it would be very unfortunate if we had to consider this bill on the floor of the house and discuss the evidence that was brought before the committee. It is not desirable that this should be done if it can possibly be avoided, and in what I say to-night I shall not refer, except to a very brief extent, to the evidence that was given and certainly not at all to those things which might seem to be objectionable. I shall object for certain other reasons. I repeat, it is very unfortunate that this bill has come back to this house for it will introduce on the floor of the house a matter which we might well avoid.
It will be pointed out of course that the bill has had the sanction of the senate; that is true. But it should also be pointed out that the bill when it was before the senate committee carried by a majority of four to three, and that in itself indicates that there was good ground for difference of opinion in the matter, and good ground at least for the private bills committee taking the position they did. The charge has been made that the members of the private bills committee did not familiarize themselves with the evidence, but that is not in accordance with the facts. I have reason to know that many members of the private bills committee who opposed this bill did familiarize themselves with the evidence. I think it is unfortunate

Clarence MacGregor Roberts
also that a certain member of the senate committee-and I might refer to him here since he has seen fit to discuss the matter and give it publicity-has followed the course he has. 1 know that under ordinary circumstances we are not allowed to refer to what has taken place in the senate; but when the chairman of the senate committee saw fit to give an interview to a Winnipeg newspaper, throwing reflections on the members of the private bills committee-
The hon. member should not refer to what has taken place in the upper house.
I am referring to what a member of the senate committee said to a Winnipeg newspaper.
It is clear that no reference should be made to proceedings in the upper house.

I bow to your ruling, Mr. Speaker, but it does seem to me that when the chairman of the senate committee sees fit to give to a Winnipeg newspaper an interview in which he casts reflections on a committee of this house I cannot be very far out of order in referring to what he has said.

Will the hon. gentleman pardon me? I was looking at the rule when he was referring to the statement made by the chairman of the senate committee; I did not know that he was referring to an article in the press or an interview which is an entirely different matter. I was speaking of proceedings in the other house when I requested the hon. member to refrain from making any reference thereto.

I have no intention of referring to anything that was said in the senate, but I think I am in order in referring to what the chairman of the senate committee said in an interview given the press. In that interview he cast reflections on the private bills committee of this house, indicating that we had not sufficiently studied the evidence, had not been reading it, and therefore should not reverse the finding of the senate committee. Now it is a matter of procedure that seems to be accepted in this house that when these bills come from the senate and get their first and second readings they are referred to the private bills committee. That seems to be the regular procedure, and if it is not competent for the private bills committee of this house to review the evidence and pass judgment in accordance with that evidence, then the whole thing becomes a farce and we might as well drop the procedure altogether.
So far as the evidence is concerned, I can assure the house that I read it myself and I know that other members of the committee read it; and when we bear in mind the fact that the bill passed the senate committee by a majority of four to three, then there is no good ground for criticism of the private bills committee because they saw fit, by a majority of eighteen or nineteen to nine, to reverse the finding of the senate committee. As I said at the outset, I do not want at this stage to go into certain features of the evidence but I do wish to refer to one fact and that is that the evidence proved that this man who is seeking the divorce from his wife at one time connived with his wife to secure a divorce, to the extent that he obtained for her a railway pass to Reno. I think he was an employee of tlhe Canadian National Railways and he may not have bought it; anyway he got it for her. Later, realizing the position in which he had put himself by appearing to connive, he withdrew the pass and then, as I understand the matter, made a pretence of objecting to her going to Reno. This of course was a foolish procedure under any circumstances. But it indicated that he was willing to secure a divorce and that he withdrew the pass and assumed an attitude of seeming opposition only because he realized-probably on the advice of his lawyer, for all we know-that he was compromising himself and that this . would work against him when the matter came before the various bodies that had to adjudicate upon the case.
It is quite true that when the bill came before the private bills committee it was indicated that we were not allowed to bring forward new evidence. That would seem to be in harmony with the legal procedure that when a case is appealed, the appeal must be based upon the evidence already submitted. I am not a lawyer, but I understand that is the situation. There was a certain type of evidence given before the senate committee that the respondents were not in a position at the time to refute. That did not, however, and does not prevent those of us who had read and studied the particular evidence in question from considering it ourselves, judging the weight of it and recalling that in many respects it was open to objection and might easily be overthrown. If we are called upon to discuss the matter before the committee of the whole house where we have to go into the case in fuller detail, then I shall be compelled-

What is the evidence?

Clarence MacGregor Roberts

I could go into it if that
were thought desirable, but at this stage 1 do not think it is. That is, I would not go into it if that could possibly be avoided, and it is only because of the motion which has been forced upon us by the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg (Mr. Ernst) that we are discussing it at all. As I have said, although the legal procedure is that we are not allowed to introduce new evidence, that does not prevent some of us at least from seeing the very weak spots in the evidence that was adduced, and probably we can base our conclusions upon the evidence as it appears to us.
I have said already that this bill has been turned down by the private bills committee, the majority who voted against the bill believing they had good grounds for rejecting the evidence that was submitted. I have pointed out already that there was abundant evidence of connivance; that it is an accepted principle that when persons come before a divorce court they must come with clean hands. It may be quite true that the plaintiff in this case was not guilty of the offence which was charged against his wife, but it was abundantly proven that he was anything but faithful to the marriage vows which he took. Therefore I express regret that the matter has been brought to the notice of the house once again, and I still further regret that we are to be compelled to go into the details of the evidence as we certainly shall be if. this motion carries and the Speaker leaves the chair for the house to go into committee of the whole.

Mr. Chairman, the only interest I have in this matter is my desire to see to it that the fair name of the private bills committee should remain unassailed. A few days ago, this bill was brought before the committee and it was rejected by a big majority. I therefore feel bound to protest as far as it is in my power against the procedure followed by the sponsors of this motion.
So, I urge upon those who are desirous of safeguarding the rights of the several committees established by this parliament for a number of years as well as upon the protectors of widows and orphans, to vote against the motion.
Before the question carries-
Thanks for the anticipation -before the question carries.

My hon. friend may make something of that point, but I do not feel about the matter exactly as he does. It is to be regretted that Quebec has not arranged that divorce cases should come before the judges of that province as they do before the judges of other provinces in this dominion, but I think it is because they do not believe in divorce. I am, always have been and always will be opposed to divorce, and if there is any evidence to justify the conclusion that in a divorce case brought before the House of Commons and the Senate the divorce should not be granted, I intend to cast my vote to that effect.
As the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown) has said, the procedure in this parliament is that a divorce bill is first considered by the upper chamber. A committee of that house considers the evidence, and after it has done so, under the constitution such divorce bills are sent to this house so that they -may be considered by a special committee of the commons. In this particular case this bill was considered by the senate, and, strange as it may seem to you, sir, and to me, we found that after the bill had been considered by the senate the divorce was approved by four members of the senate committee as opposed to three. I realize with you, sir, that as a member of the House of Commons I have no right, nor has any other member a right, to criticize anything that may happen in the other chamber, but I just wish to direct the attention of hon. members to the difference between the way in which the matter was considered by the committee in the other chamber and the way in which the members of the private bills committee of this house considered it.
The bill came to the members of the private bills committee. I have the honour of being a member of that committee. And may I say that outside of myself that committee is perhaps one of the strongest in the House of Commons. The members of that committee take their duties seriously. Whether it is a divorce bill or any other bill which comes before that committee, we endeavour to give to the measure under review the best consideration possible and make our findings accordingly. Much as I, and I think perhaps I may speak for other members of the committee, dislike it, we had to deal with this particular divorce case. Like my hon. friend from Lisgar-and again I am sure I am voicing the sentiments of a number of other members of the committee-we were obliged, contrary to our inclination but as our duty to the house and to the public, to read the evidence in the

Clarence MacGregor Roberts
case It is not a pleasant duty as far as I am concerned, and I cannot understand the attitude of anyone who, the committee having decided the matter to the best of their ability and agreed upon a decision practically in camera, would now compel us to discuss this thing before the public in the House of Commons.
It is not in camera; it is wide open.

I know it is wide open, but
as everyone knows, in that committee the same publicity is not given to a bill of this kind as would be given if it were considered in the House of Commons. What I am trying to say is that with regard to bills relating to divorce it is to be regretted that this House of Commons, or even the Senate, more mature as they are than we, should have to adjudicate on bills of this kind. However, as the hon. member for Lisgar said, the private bills committee of the House of Commons did go into the matter as thoroughly as possible. We considered the evidence; we heard the arguments of solicitors both for petitioner and for respondent, and, after considering every angle of the situation, by a majority of I think eighteen to nine decided not to adopt the preamble of the bill, and the chairman of the committee so reported to this house. It is true that this report has not yet been concurred in, but under the rules I understand that is not necessary. However, in opening cur mail this morning we found that someone had put in our box in the post office a memorandum addressed to the members of the House of Commons. As far as I am concerned I have no objection to anyone who feels he has a grievance addressing me either personally or through the mail. But there are some things in this memorandum or statement to which I object. It is signed by the petitioner, C. M. Roberts, and it refers to senate bill M. He says first:
This bill was rejected by the private bills committee of the House of Commons on March 28, 1935, after the senate had recommended that the petitioner be divorced from his wife.
That statement of course is correct, and to my mind this is very important because except under very unusual circumstances it has always been a rule of this house that when a special committee appointed by the house to deal with any matter goes into it thoroughly and reports a certain finding, the house adopts the finding of the committee. This bill, as Mr. Roberts says in this memorandum, was rejected by the private bills
committee of the House of Commons on March 28, 1935. I respectfully submit to my fellow members, and to members of other committees who expect us to agree to their findings and concur in any report which they make to this house, that the same courtesy is due to the members of the private bills committee. We rejected that bill after going into the evidence and hearing what was to be said for or against the petitioner and respondent. But that does not satisfy the gentleman who signed this memorandum. He goes on to say:
A few minutes before the private bills committee assembled, an unsigned memorandum was delivered to the members, which contained many definitely inaccurate statements not in accordance either with the facts or with the evidence taken before the senate committee, but designed to detract from petitioner's character and not only to prejudice the minds of the committee in favour of respondent but to mislead and deceive the members of it.
Now, sir, it seems to me that no person who comes before either the Senate or the House of Commons committee has any right to insinuate that members of the private bills committee were at that time or at any time influenced by letters or memoranda received by them. Consequently the petitioner puts himself in a very awkward position as far as I am concerned, and I think perhaps in the view of other members of the committee, when he signs a statement of that kind and dares to insinuate that members of that private bills committee were influenced by any statement which was handed to them or passed around in the committee. Perhaps the reason this Mr. Roberts now passes this memorandum around is to get square with whoever it was who circulated the previous memorandum in the private bills committee. But I say, and again I think I am voicing the sentiments of every member of the committee who dealt with this matter, that we were not influenced in the slightest degree by the memorandum which was passed around or which we found in our places when we met that morning.
But Mr. Roberts is not satisfied with that. He goes on to say:
The petitioner submits that a serious miscarriage of justice would result if the attitude of the majority of the private bills committee were approved by the house, and humbly brings the matter to the attention of the members of the House of Commons in order that this miscarriage of justice may be rectified.
Sir, that is a bold statement to make. Perhaps it would be as well if in some way Mr. Roberts were caused to appear before the bar of this house, because he practically says here that a serious miscarriage of justice would re-
Clarence MacGregor Roberts

suit if the attitude of the majority of the private bills committee were approved by the house. My hon. friend here says that perhaps he should be summoned in order to apologize for his statement that the private bills committee caused a miscarriage of justice when they decided, eighteen to .nine, that this divorce should not be granted. It certainly is contempt of this house, if I may put it that way. But let me go on further. The statement says:
The following remarks respecting allegations made in the memorandum in question and in the private bills committee are respectfully submitted:
1. Before the senate committee the act of adultery was proven definitely by three reliable witnesses whose evidence was unshaken in cross examination and accepted by the senate.
I have not the slightest wish to criticize the decision of the senate. I am quite willing that the gentleman who signs this memorandum take whatever comfort he can from the fact that four senators out of seven decided that the act was committed in this instance. While it is quite possible that an act of adultery was proven in this case, anyone reading the evidence submitted to the private bills committee must come to the conclusion that the gentleman who signs this memorandum should hang his head in shame both as far as his own actions are concerned and as regards his conduct towards his wife, whom he wanted to divorce. Then he goes on:
The evidence of respondent and co-respondent in denial is valueless. The record shows various instances where they have directly contradicted themselves when confronted with sworn statements made in the Montreal courts, and the fact that they deceived petitioner by going to Maine and living in the same house for two weeks is conclusive as to their relationship.
Well, sir, if I remember the evidence correctly this is only a matter of the kettle calling the pot black. As my hon. friend from Lisgar stated previously, anyone appealing to the law, even if it is in connection with a divorce, at least should come with clean hands. Then he goes on:
The evidence further shows that during the fall of 1933, the respondent and co-respondent continuously went out together-
There is not much harm in that; it does not prove anything. Evidently this man Roberts was jealous; perhaps he was not as young as his wife, and became jealous because she went out with someone else.
Order.

What is wrong with that? Of course the bachelors in this house may object

to that; that reminds me of a story I once heard about a friend of mine in Nova Scotia, but I cannot tell it here. I do say, however, in all decency that this should not be broadcast in this house; it should go to the private bills committee for consideration, if it is to be considered at all. Then the next clause reads:
While there had previously been some question of her husband's consent to a Reno divorce, that idea was entirely abandoned by petitioner, nevertheless, respondent proceeded to Reno against her husband's direct orders, and' secured a divorce.
According to my recollection of the evidence that statement is absolutely incorrect. I have not looked up the evidence since I received this memorandum, but if I remember it correctly this Mr. Roberts induced his wife to go to Reno. He obtained a railway pass for her and induced her to go to Reno to get a divorce, so how can he now come and endeavour to have this house reconsider the matter by telling us that his wife went to Reno to get a divorce without the consent of her husband? Then he goes on to say:
On return from Reno her effects were moved to an apartment by co-respondent and it was only some time after that removal that she took an action in separation against her husband and secured the right to a separate domicile. The co-respondent visited her practically daily at this apartment.
Quite possible this woman did move to another apartment, and as I remember the evidence she had every reason in the world to do so. I believe in another country there is a ground for divorce known as mental cruelty. If in this country we granted divorces for mental cruelty, to my mind this woman would be entitled to a divorce rather than her husband.
Elucidate.

I don't like to tell all the dirt in this matter. Paragraph 4 reads:
The report of the proceedings before the senate committee shows that that body was satisfied that the relations of the petitioner and Miss X (referred to in the memorandum) were entirely innocent and the reference in the memorandum is clearly an attempt to exaggerate a harmless incident in order to divert attention from the flagrant misconduct definitely proven against the respondent.
I direct your attention, Mr. Speaker, to the difference between the clause I have just read and the clause which precedes it. In clause 3 this man says that after his wife moved from- his apartment the co-respondent visited her practically daily. Then in clause 4 this man refers to a certain Miss X, whoever she may be. I do not want to know her name, God knows, and I hope no one else wants to

Clarence MacGregor Roberts
know it, especially the bald headed men in this chamber. But this man admits in clause 4 that the evidence given before the senate committee, as appearing at page 17 of the proceedings-and I should like my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Hanson) to read page 17 for himself-shows that that body was satisfied that the relations of the petitioner, Mr. C. M. Roberts, and Miss X, referred to in the memorandum, were entirely innocent, and I hope they were. I want to say, however, that if the petitioner and Miss X could walk around the streets of Montreal, go to moving pictures, have five o'clock tea and so on, all in a harmless way, why should this man who signs this memorandum want us as members of this house to believe that because the wife also walked around with another gentleman she was committing an indecent act, if I may put it in that way? Then he goes on:
The statement is absolutely untrue that petitioner introduced respondent to co-respondent in the spring of 1933 with a view to throwing them together.
Evidently, whoever did it, there was some throwing together of some kind, either by the husband or by the wife or by both of them. The evidence of the respondent is that she met the co-respondent in February, 1933. If my hon. friends want to look into this evidence they will find it at pages 63, 75 and 76. Then paragraph 6 follows, and let us not forget that this man is referring to his wife, the woman whom he promised to love-
Honour, and obey.

She promised to honour and
obey him, I presume, but when he married her he promised to love and protect her. Here is what he says about her in paragraph 6:
The statement that Mrs. Roberts went out with the co-respondent in order to show petitioner the folly of his ways is absolutely false. On the morning of August 5, 1933, the husband saw his wife off at Bonaventure station, and gave her a pass to go to Maine for a holiday.
If he had any suspicion of this woman why did he get a pass and send her to Maine for a holiday? It does seem to me if he was of this suspicious nature he might at least keep his weather eye cocked, if hon. members know what I mean, and not get a pass for her and send her to the state of Maine. Evidently he did not trust her very far, because he states'
(She left the train at St. Lambert a mile or two out of Montreal and stayed there until next day and then went to Portland by motor with co-respondent, and remained with him in the same hoarding house for two weeks and returned with him all unknown to her husband and for the purpose of deceiving him.
He must have found out, at some time, whether at that particular moment or shortly afterwards, that she stopped off at St. Lambert. He must have found out that she was in this boarding house with the co-respondent for a period of two weeks. Although he pretends it was unknown to him and was done for the purpose of deceiving him, I wonder how in the name of heaven he found it out in the first place. The least he could have done would have been to come before the committee of the Senate or the committee of the House of Commons and state how he found all this out.
The next clause is not very important. He denies the statement that the husband owed his wife $4,000. Well, with most of us it is the other way about. I think she should be congratulated upon being able to get $4,000 out of her husband, whether it was for the purpose of going to Maine, to Reno or for any other purpose. Then he states:
She forced him by threat of suit to pay her

Well, if he owed her that money, why should he not pay it? What particular objection does he raise because he owed his wife money and she asked him for it. When he would not give it to her willingly she forced him to pay $1,000.
Then he winds up this wonderful document with some further observations. Before voting to throw this nasty mess into the maelstrom of public controversy, hon. members should hear the whole story. He states:
The petitioner is entitled' to have the facts of his ease decided upon the sworn testimony of the witnesses and to have the benefit of the affirmative finding of the senate committee before whom those witnesses were heard, and who could judge of their credibility by their demeanour.
Let me deal with that phase of the matter. Earlier in my observations I stated that I have no more objection to a decision made by the senate than would an hon. member learned in the law to a decision made by the supreme court. When a supreme court gives a decision either for or against-and it must be for one and against the other-no objection is made if either client decides to appeal to the supreme court in banco, consisting of six or seven judges. It often happens that while the one judge in the lower court has the opportunity of hearing the evidence, the supreme court in banco, without hearing the evidence, just as the private bills committee in this instance, decide to reverse the decision made by the one judge. This man has no right in any document to insinuate that because the members of the

279S
Clarence MacGregor Roberts

private bills committee did not hear the evidence given by the witnesses they are not in a position to give a proper decision. The judges in the supreme court in banco or in the Supreme Court of Canada decide cases on evidence submitted to them in writing. Just so I say we as the members of the private bills committee have an equal right to give a judgment, whether it be good or bad, on the evidence which we may read. Perhaps I would not take so strong a stand if this matter had been decided by a full committee of the senate. Had there been as many members on the senate committee which heard the evidence as there were on the committee of the House of Commons, perhaps I would be willing to forego some of my views and to agree that after all, with their wide experience, hon. members of the senate may have been right. However in View of the fact that only seven members of the senate made this decision and some twenty-seven members of the House of Commons reversed it, I say this man is not acting fairly when in the memorandum he practically states that the members of the private bills committee did not give his case proper consideration.
Here is a worse insinuation:
The petitioner does not impugn the good faith of members of the committee whose votes were cast against his bill, but earnestly submits that their good faith was imposed upon.
I will admit that the lady was present, but I insist that we were not induced to make our findings because our good faith had been imposed upon. Two gentlemen learned in the law represented the respective sides of she case, and presented strong arguments. In my view one counsel did not have as good a case as the other, and the majority of the committee decided the divorce should not be granted. When this man states that our good faith was imposed upon in arriving at a decision I submit this House of Commons should back up the members of the private bills committee. Every hon. member of this chamber, no matter how he may feel in the matter, in view of the fact that this man has made such a statement, should stand behind the committee which went into the matter, considered the evidence and gave a decision to the best of their ability.
In my humble manner, in my modest way, I have endeavoured to state the views of the private bills committee. In view of all the circumstances I appeal to my fellow members not to reopen the matter. I am opposed to divorces. So long as I am a member of this parliament and have to deal with divorce

cases, if at all possible I shall refuse divorces. In cases of trouble between man and wife I believe it is my duty and that of other hon. members to try to get these people to reconcile their differences and to live together as God and man intended they should.
' Mr. MICHAEL LUCHKOVICH (Vegre-ville): Mr. Speaker, I hope that the time will some day come when we can throw divorce out of parliament altogether and hand it over if possible to the Exchequer Court of Canada. I was one of the committee of three that was appointed to be a witness to the hearings of most of these divorce cases that are being heard by the senate committee, and I can assure you that what I hear down there is worse than a lot of the true stories that are printed in the True Story magazine.
The first objection that is made in this circular that has been sent to members of the House of Commons is that a few minutes before the private bills committee assembled, an unsigned memorandum was delivered to the members. The lawyers for the petitioner complained before the committee that the members had received a circular from the. respondent, and they objected to that, and yet they are doing the very same thing in this circular. I think that what is sauce for the gander should be sauce for the goose as well. I myself feel that there has been connivance in this case. In Bourinot, fourth edition, at page 637 I find this passage:
Connivance, condonation or collusion, a ground for rejection-In such cases the Minister of Justice may intervene.
"If adultery be proved', the party from whom the divorce is sought may nevertheless be admitted to prove connivance at, or condonation of the adultery, collusion in the proceedings for divorce, or adultery on the part of the petitioner.
Connivance at. or condonation of the adultery, or collusion in the proceedings for the divorce, is always a sufficient ground for rejecting a bill of divorce, and shall be inquired into by the committee, and should the committee have reason to suspect connivance or collusion, and in their opinion it is desirable that fuller inquiry should be made, such opinion and the reasons therefor shall be communicated to the Minister of Justice, that he may intervene and oppose the bill should the interest of public justice in his opinion call for such intervention."
There is no doubt in my mind that there has been connivance all the way by the petitioner. The very fact that he sent his wife to Reno, asking her to go down there and get a divorce, is connivance -to my mind, and if connivance is a defence I cannot see how the senate committee could have passed the divorce.

Clarence MacGregor Roberts
Will the hon. member permit a question? Will he indicate where in the evidence there is shown to be any connivance with respect to the particular act on which this petition is based?

Yes I will, but I have only five minutes more, and I shall have to do it after the Easter recess.
There is another passage in Bourinot which presents the views of Senator Gowan, who in 1888 said, as will be found in Bourinot at page 628:
-for the decisions of the House of Lords on bills of divorce have not the weight that attaches to the regular legal tribunals. The majority determines, and in a minority on a vote may be found men of learning, wisdom and experience, expressing opinions adverse to the determination, more in accordance with the eternal principles of truth and justice.
This divorce did pass the senate committee by a vote of four to three. Nevertheless there were three members on the senate divorce committee who thought fit, on the grounds I will say of truth and justice or humanity, to cast their votes against this divorce.
The circumstances of the reintroduction of this bill into the house vary somewhat from the circumstances of the divorce bill which was introduced into the house last year. I refer to the Stotland divorce bill of last year which was defeated in the House of Commons and was afterwards reintroduced by the member for Ottawa (Mr. Chevrier). At page 4298 of last year's Hansard I find that it was negatived1 by the house, so that we are discussing this divorce case at this time more or less on the sufferance of the house.
As far as the evidence given in the senate committee is concerned respecting the chief offence on which the divorce is based, I frankly say, Mr. Speaker, that I would give more credence to the evidence of witnesses who are not detectives than I would to the evidence of detectives, and in my opinion the evidence given in this case was of a nature which did not prove that the main offence on which the divorce is based was committed. I do not believe that was proved before the senate committee. As a previous speaker has said, there was an attempt made to show that because the respondent had gone to some place in Maine, that was evidence of the offence in question. The evidence also shows that the petitioner had been running around with some lady whom 92582-178}
he calls Miss X, and1 possibly he might have called her Madame X. The circular No. 4 of C. M. Roberts says:
The relations of the petitioner and* Miss X referred to were entirely innocent.
He has no more right to say that on his own behalf than the wife has to testify similarly on her behalf.
