speechtext:
Hon. H. A. STEWART (Minister of Public Works) moved the second reading of Bill No. 63, to create employment by public works and undertakings throughout Canada and to authorize the guarantee of certain railway equipment securities.
He said:	Mr. Speaker, the established
practice of this house on the second reading of a bill is to confine the discussion to the principle involved. I feel satisfied that I can safely say, in view of the action taken last session in regard to a similar bill and the discussion that has already taken place on the resolution, that the principle of the bill meets with general favour, whether or not there may be criticism of some of its sections or of some of the details. There was upon the resolution a pretty comprehensive discussion not only of the principle of the bill but of the details, and I would hope that that will have the effect of shortening the discussion both on the second reading and on the bill when it gets into committee of the whole.
I have no desire to labour the matter or to delay the passing of the second reading. I believe every hon. gentleman realizes that the object of the bill is to provide employment over a wide field and that it is desired that employment should be afforded at the earliest possible moment. I should sincerely hope that without restricting the rights and privileges of any member or limiting the discussion it might be found possible to give this bill all its readings to-night in order that the object which we all have in view may be attained. I therefore move that the bill be read the second time.

connection with the point raised by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie), I suggest to the minister that it would be well to have the Minister of Marine (Mr. Duranleau) here to lay on the table

certain supplementary orders in council which he promised some days ago to lay before this committee. On the orders of the day some days ago I called the attention of the minister to orders in council in which there was not the information which I believe the committee should have. Take for instance order in council under the Public Works Construction Act, P.C. 1564, page 6 of sessional paper 104VV, dated April 12, 1935. This order in council provides that Mr. Ernest Gohier, consulting engineer of Montreal, should be authorized to prepare certain plans of works at Three Rivers. The order in council recites that Mr. Gohier has already designed and successfully carried out extensive works in the harbour of Three Rivers, and therefore in consideration of this the minister recommends that he be authorized to employ Mr. Gohier to prepare plans and supervise the construction of works provided for at Three Rivers " on the terms and conditions embodied in the form of agreement hereto attached," and that he be authorized to execute with Mr. Gohier a contract in the said form. The terms and conditions said to be attached are not attached to the order in council, and the same thing applies to a number of these orders. I submit to the Minister of Public Works that this is not adequate information on which this committee can base a judgment as to whether or not these contracts have been properly carried out.
I do not wish to renew the discussion we had a few evenings ago with respect to the painting of the bridge in Montreal. It is recited in that order in council, P.C. 1869, page 21 of the same sessional paper, that a certain number of firms-International Paints (Canada) Limited; Canada Paint Company, Limited; Thorpe-Hamforock Company, Limited-submitted tenders, all at the same price, namely, $2.90 per gallon red lead, and so on. Further on, the order in council states that the minister recommends that he be authorized to enter into contracts with International Paints of Canada, Limited, Canada Paint Company, Limited, and Thorpe-Hambrock Company, Limited, for the supplying of what paint is required, but it does not say what proportion of the supplies is to be taken from each of these companies. It simply states that he is to be authorized to enter into contracts with these three companies. I assume that the supply was divided

Public Works Program
in some proportions. In the same order in council it is stated that certain firms submitted quotations in accordance with the conditions laid down " as indicated below and in the attached schedule." These companies are Southern Working Company, Limited; Federated Construction Company, Limited; F. J. Leduc and Associates; Nicole Gentile; L. Knight; R. F. Walsh and Company, Limited; James Pitcher; C. J. Pott Company, Limited. It does not say anywhere what prices these firms submitted. It then goes on to say:
After investigating we are satisfied that lowest tender for application of paint to bridge, not having been accompanied by accepted cheque, should not be considered, particularly as reports of his financial position are most unsatisfactory.
I would like to know who the lowest tenderer was, because it is not stated. It goes on a little later to recommend that an order in council be entered into with Leduc and his associates. Whereas in pursuance of the said act there are dominion public works throughout Canada in process of construction amounting approximately to $30,000,000-
And the bill itself is called the Supplementary Public Works Construction Act, 1935. Therefore the two are linked up, altogether apart, I suggest, from the very natural desire which the minister may have of satisfying all the members of the house that everything which was done under the provisions of last year's act was carried out properly and in a manner which would be quite satisfactory to him and his associates, the other ministers who are now acting ministers of public works in their various departments. I am sorry that I cannot agree with my hon. friend. If he wants to raise a point of order, let him do so. I think I am quite within my rights in discussing on this supplementary public works construction bill, the preamble of which contains a reference to the works now going on, the lack of information, calling the attention of the minister to the fact- that we have not as yet any information as to the manner in which last year's Public Works Construction Act was carried out. We have before us orders in council which do not give information and which I am sorry to say are extremely badly drafted. I do not want to go the length of saying that this is done by design, that it is intended to hide the information; but when one finds that almost every second or third order in council does not give the information to which the committee is entitled, I think we have a right to protest and to say to the minister: Well, if that is the way in which you are going to carry on with your new public works construction act, we want to know. I am not protesting very much-I think there is a great deal of cant and hypocrisy about all this business- against hon. gentlemen opposite now that they are in power using their political influence and power to help their friends; they would do that anyway. I am not going to make any bones about the matter; I would like them to admit it. I rather approve the attitude of the
Public Works Program,

Minister of Marine; there is not much hypocrisy about him. He comes out boldly and says: You chaps did that in Quebec; I am going to do the same thing; I am going to help my friends. I am willing to say right now that he will get a great deal of credit for saying so. I am not complaining so much about that Let them come out and admit it. I will give my hon. friend an instance. In reading over these orders in council, what do I find? These works are supposed to be for the benefit of the unemployed, presumably of the poorer categories of the unemployed, the poor workmen who have no jobs. I was looking over the orders in council which referred to Halifax. That locality is far away from my home and my reference to it cannot hurt anybody in my constituency, so I thought I might discuss Halifax, but it is an example of what has happened all the way through. On page 33 of this sessional paper 104VV, I find under an order in council of September 7. certain items of the Public Works Construction Act, numbers 62 to 70, were placed under the Department of Marine; that is to say, the works are enumerated and the administration, management of construction of the public works mentioned in schedule A were placed under the Department of Marine. Bennett, acting chief engineer of the harbour commissioners of Halifax in an engineering capacity, and the harbour commissioners of Halifax in a supervising capacity, all without remuneration, in connection with the works to be carried out under items 62 to 70. I do not want to read all the orders in council, but I mention that.
I find that on page 59 with respect to item 67. the Halifax harbour contract was awarded to the McDonald Construction Company and that the commission received $730.43 for supervision and engineering. Then on page 61 with respect to item 66. a contract was awarded to the McDonald Construction Company and the sum of $881.50 was allotted to

the harbour commission for engineering and
supervision which they had already agreed to do without remuneration. Then on page 72, items 68 and 69, a fairly large contract was awarded to the John S. Metcalf Company, Limited, to carry on the work of a grain elevator. Going up 1 Then on page 77 I find another contract was awarded, another of the items to be looked after by the Halifax harbour commission and by its chief engineer without remuneration: item 64, contract awarded to T. C. Gorman (Nova Scotia) Limited, and the Halifax harbour commission obtained two and a half per cent, something like $20,000 for supervision-work which they were supposed to do without remuneration.
And this is the best of all. This is really pretty good. After the Halifax harbour commission is given I would say about $50,000, on page 84 I read this. This is after the contracts were all let. Order in council of April 2, 1935 says:
The committee of the privy council on the recommendation of the Minister of Marine, advise that in connection with the works to be carried out in Halifax harbour under items 62 to 70-
All of which were already provided for.
-he be authorized to employ Mr. E. H. James of Montreal as consulting engineer at a fee of $1,000 per month, the total amount for his services not to exceed $9,000 and to be charg-able against any of the above items.
So that we have first the Marine department with its engineers to look after these works, then the Halifax harbour commission with its engineers to look after these works without remuneration; yet on every single contract they obtained remuneration, and then, apparently not satisfied with the people of Halifax, they employed this man James at $1,000 a month. This will explain why I want certain information with respect to other orders in council.
I find in looking through this that a Mr. Ernest Gohier of Montreal was employed to look after the works in Quebec harbour as consulting engineer, after the same practice or procedure had been gone through, namely the Marine department being put in charge

Public Works Program
with their engineers, then the Quebec harbour commission with its engineers-it is as supervisor that they have prepared the plans; then Ernest Gohier is appointed at a fee of $1,500. And not satisfied with that, Mr. Bigonesse is appointed as an architect at a fee of $4,000. I find also that Mr. Gohier was employed with respect to the work in Three Rivers harbour, but they do not say at what fee. And with respect to the Chicoutimi harbour, although there the department had engineers, this same Mr. Gohier was also employed. The minister shakes his head. Does he want me to read the order in council?

speechtext:
By shaking my head
I am only telling my friend that he is mistaken when he states that these harbour commissions have engineers. subtopic: WORKS, UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OF RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT

That is one explanation, but it hardly justifies the minister in employing Mr. Gohier for Quebec, where they have a highly paid engineer and a very good one. Nor does it justify his employing Mr. James of Montreal to supervise the work in Halifax harbour, where the work was already done, the contracts had been let, the plans prepared. I should like to know-perhaps only as a matter of curiosity, but I think the working men of Chicoutimi and Three Rivers and Quebec and Halifax would like to know-what Mr. Ernest Gohier's fee is. The minister said a few nights ago that he is a very reputable engineer, and I am quite willing to agree with that, although I do not know anything about him; but he is getting a mighty big fee for work at Quebec done by someone else. I should like to know what fee he is getting for Chicoutimi -it is not stated in the order in council-also what fee he is getting for Three Rivers. I think if the minister were fair he would tell us. The order in council in respect to Three Rivers says:
The minister recommends that he be authorized to contract for the services of Mr. Ernest Gohier-
He has already contracted for them, and at $15,000 for Quebec. I would like to know what contract he made for the other places. I suggest that we should have this information to see how much is being given to high-salaried men.

subtopic: WORKS, UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OF RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Was Mr. Bigonesse paid for Quebec also?

subtopic: WORKS, UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OF RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
There are two orders in council covering his work, one for the same job as Mr. Gohier is doing in Quebec harbour 

Mr. Bigonesse gets $4,000 for that-and another speaks of employing him as architect on some contract at the Quebec observatory. It recommends that "he be engaged in this connection on the terms and conditions set forth in the attached memorandum." But the memorandum is not attached. I think the workers who are supposed to benefit from this would be interested in knowing how much these men are getting. Before we proceed further with this we ought to know how much of this money is going to high salaried men. As I said at the outset, I am not protesting so much about the manner in which the contracts have been let, or making complaint about the minister helping his friends. But I do think that it is beyond reason to ask this house to vote such extremely large salaries in this time of depression. I may be all wrong, but I suggest that since Mr. Gohier is getting $15,000 for Quebec, on the same basis he would probably be getting $5,000 more for Three Rivers and $5,000 more for Chicoutimi. Perhaps he is getting only $5,000 for the two, but even that would make a $20,000 salary, which is a pretty good thing for looking after three contracts. It is a bigger salary than the Prime Minister has for looking after the whole of Canada, a bigger salary than any minister of the crown gets for running a government department. I should like, before I proceed further, to have some explanation from the minister on that point.

But we have to pay the commission -not the commissioners, not the engineer,- we have to pay the commission for their employees. They put on the job three or four or five or six employees; surely the harbour commission is entitled to get out of this vote the salaries of these employees, and that relieves the commission of so much in its administration costs. There is no expense to the country, the administration expenses of the harbour commission being reduced accordingly. The harbour commissioners receive the very same salary that

As Mr. Gohier, he is representing my department at Three Rivers, at Chicoutimi and also at Quebec as I have no chief engineer. When my hon. friend says he is getting a larger salary than a cabinet minister, surely he knows better than that; he knows what are the expenses of an engineer; he has to keep a place of business, to employ a staff for the drafting of plans, specifications, details and so forth. My hon. friends very quickly forget what happened under their administration with regard to engineering. We have not spent half what was spent by my hon. friends when they were in power, from 1926 to 1930, in engineering fees. I want to add this:
My hon. friend says we are paying Mr. James
81,000	a month to supervise the works in Halifax. I think the expense is quite reasonable when it is considered that these works are costing a large amount. I think it is fitting that we get the best architects or engineers to supervise the work and to examine the plans and specifications. The hon. member knows what occurred in the city of Quebec in connection with the pier built at Wolfe's Cove by hon. members opposite. Since 1930 we had to make an expenditure of over 8100,000 to prevent that pier from slipping into the river. If the work had been properly planned and built under the supervision of a man of wide experience in under-water operations, probably we would not have had to spend so much when we took office. That pier was built during the years 1928 and 1929, and in the early part of the year 1930. I claim it is good policy to employ the best possible engineers when under-water operations valued at many millions of dollars have to be carried out.

subtopic: WORKS, UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OF RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
I am not going to discuss
the engineering feals which the minister performed in connection with saving Quebec harbour. At some other time we shall be quite willing to vote a few dollars with which to build him a monument to be placed alongside of those of Champlain, Jacques Cartier and others. In those days we carried out harbour works of considerable magnitude, looking to the future development of the harbour. We spent money; at the present moment I am not particularly anxious to enter into a discussion of whether or not we wasted money. The fact is, however, that we spent money and built harbours. We were not carrying out those works for the purpose of relieving unemployment, whereas in the present instance that is what is being done. I do not believe it was ever the intention of parliament that these unemployment works should provide employment for high salaried men. Such men are not to be classed as unemployed, in the commonly accepted sense of the term.
Let us return to the minister's discussion with respect to Halifax. Order in council P.C. 2110 at page 34 states that the minister-
-be authorized to employ the services of C. S. Bennett, acting chief engineer of the harbour commissioners of Halifax in an engineering capacity, and the harbour commissioners of Halifax in a supervising capacity, all without remuneration.
That is what they had. I could refer to five or six contracts, but I shall take only one of them. The details are fully set forth with regard to Halifax. P.C. 26, dated January 31, 1935, gives authority to enter into a contract with T. C. Gorman (Nova Scotia) Limited. It states:
The minister therefore recommends:
1.	That he be authorized to enter into a contract with Messrs. T. C. Gorman (Nova Scotia) Limited for doing the work contemplated above at an estimated cost of $259,366.80;
2.	That the Halifax harbour commission be allowed' for engineering inspection and administration and general office expenses two and a quarter per cent of the contract price.
In this case that item came to about
820.000.	I have not the exact figure, but I do know the contract was let for 8259,366.80.
In connection with another contract more details are given. I have before me P.C.
Public Works Program

3223 appearing at page 75, and awarded to J. P. Porter and Sons, St. Catharines, as follows:
That the acting chief engineer of the Halifax harbour commission further reports the necessity for the following additional expenditures:
(a)	for engineering and inspection approximately five per cent, $13,959.75.
(b)	administration and general office expense, one and a half per cent, $4,397.32.
So \Ve find more than 820,000 given for work which apparently the Halifax harbour commission had undertaken to do for nothing. Then on top of that the minister employs a man at $1,000 per month. There is no other way of getting out of it. I believe the minister is a little bit extravagant in these distressing days. A few moments ago he said, poor man, that he has no engineer in his department, no deputy and no assistants which he should have. For that reason he has to go outside to get that assistance. Strangely enough, however, his engineer seems to do a lot of work, this poor unfortunate fellow who does not count for very much. For instance, I see that the acting chief engineer of the Department of Marine certified " that the work is of such a nature that it may be more beneficially executed by day labour." When we come to Quebec contracts we find he has more engineers than you could shake a stick at.
I now turn to P.C. 2824 at page 45, an item for Quebec. Perhaps I would do well to read nearly all of it. Dated November 8, 1934, it states:
The committee of the privy council have had before them a report, dated 6th November, 1934, from the Minister of Marine, stating with respect to the construction of new transit sheds to replace old sheds 24 and 25 on pier No. 1 of the Quebec harbour commission at Quebec, as provided for in item No. 137 of the Public Works Construction Act, 1934, as follows: -
1.	That consequent upon the authority obtained in order in council of the 15th August, 1934 (P.C. 1801), the Quebec harbour commissioners were instructed to invite tenders for this work:
2.	That the tenders received in response to this invitation were not considered satisfactory:
3.	That fresh tenders were subsequently invited by the Minister of Marine from the following _ contractors, who submitted quotations as indicated below:-
Tlelphe Maranda, Ksq.. Que.. P.Q.. $389,989.
Romeo Vachon, Esq., Que., P.Q., $409,154.
Colonial Construction Co., Ltd., Que., P.Q., $420,149.
Joseph Nolin. Esq., Que., P.Q., $423,855.
Amedee Latulippe. Esq.. Que.. P.Q.. $478,090.
Amedee Demers, Esq., Que., P.Q., $479,489.
Abel Ratte. Esq., Que.. P.Q., $485,153.
Morton Engineering & Dry Dock Co., Que., P.Q.. did not quote.
Frontenac Lumber Co., Que., P.Q., did not quote.

Cummings Construction Co., Monte Bello, P.Q., did not quote.
That as the lowest tender, which was submitted by Mr. Delphe Maranda, was still considered to be high, the minister has been in conference with him and as a result Mr. Maranda has agreed to carry out the work strictly in accordance with the plans and specifications prepared by the engineer of the harbour commissioners of Quebec, for the sum of $354,754.92, which price, in the opinion of the engineers of the Quebec harbour commission. the consulting engineer, and the acting chief engineer of the Department of Marine is fair and just.
Here is a case where the minister had three good engineers on the job so he cannot complain that he was left alone and helpless. He had the plans prepared by the engineer of the Quebec harbour commission; then he hired a consulting engineer, and the Quebec harbour commission engineer said that it was just, the consulting engineer said that it was just and the chief engineer said that it was just. How it was that the architect was not called in to say it was just I do not know. He must be a stiff-necked fellow, or he would have said that it was just.
The consulting engineer, who comes from Montreal, reports that Mr. Maranda is a contractor of twenty years' experience.

speechtext:
I am not supporting what my hon. friend from Quebec East says. I do not agree with him. I do not object to a Montreal man being there, but it was not necessary to go to Montreal to get a man to report that Mr. Maranda was a contractor of twenty years' experience and fully qualified to do this work. That report could have been made by somebody in Quebec who knew Mr. Maranda. There was no need to go to Montreal. So far as I know, all his life Mr. Maranda has been a Quebecker and doubtless he was introduced to Mr. Gohier only two or

Public Works Program
three days before Mr. Gohier made this report on him. It would have been far better to ask Mr. Tremblay or even the acting engineer of the Marine department what Mr. Maranda's
qualifications were, which I admit were extremely high.
Then the order in council goes on to ask for authority:
As the consulting engineer to the Quebec harbour commissioners and the acting chief engineer of the Department of Marine recommend that a competent architect to supervise the purely architectural details of the structure be employed, authority be granted for the employment of Mr. j. Aurele Bigonesse of Quebec as supervising architect in connection therewith at a fee of $4,000.
So there we had three engineers, and they used two strangers. But there is more about these engineers when the new contract was awarded later on to Mr. Maranda. This is a very long order in council, P.C. 322, March 18, 1935, page 81 of the sessional papers, and I shall quote only those portions which refer to the employment of engineers. I am not for a moment criticizing the government for having first told Mr. Maranda that his tender was too high, or for the minister having a conference with him and suggesting a lower tender. But now by this order in council they have recourse to the old, old game of giving Mr. Maranda an extra. That game is pretty well played out, and I expected better of the minister. When this cabinet of real politicians was formed we thought we might have a national cabinet of politicians without hypocrisy and without cant. No doubt the minister would like to be able to say, " To the victor belongs the spoils." He will support that particular kind of politics, I have no doubt, and a great many on this side will also, but we will have to get a minister who will not resort to the old-fashioned trick of camouflage by giving extras.
In any case in this particular contract they mention Mr. Gohier as being the consulting engineer. They also say that the Minister of Marine called for tenders, that plans and specifications were prepared by the engineers of the Quebec harbour commission, that a contract was entered into with Mr. Delphe Maranda, and that the engineer, Mr. Gohier -apparently he is now promoted to be engineer in chief-"reports as follows"; then there is a long report saying that the engineer recommends that a change be made in the plans and specifications and be embodied in Mr. Maranda's contract, and Mr. Maranda obtained this extra work. I do not know whether the extra amounts to $26,000 or
$181,000; it is difficult to make out. Then the order m council goes on to say:
The acting chief engineer of the Department of Marine concurs.
The engineer of the harbour commission appears to have been eliminated altogether The committee of the privy council, on the recommendation of the Minister of Marine, also concurred in the change in Mr. Maranda's contract. So I do not think the minister's complaint that he has not engineering services is really well founded, for he has three engineers on each job, or two at all events apart from the consulting engineer. Even if Mr. Swan got a lot of money I do not think the minister will be able to justify the payment of $15,000 and $20,000, and $1,000 a month in another case, to engineers when the work was already being supervised by other competent men. I suggest that to the minister, not so much by way of criticism of the past, but so that he will not carry on that policy under this new public works bill which is before the house to-night. This new bill, I submit, will not be popular in the country if in the carrying out of the work the same policy is followed that was adopted last year. I repeat that I am not criticizing the minister in regard to the general principles, if I may call them principles, which he has followed, but I am criticizing him for not having made every dollar which was spent go to the people who were most in need of it. That is the general principle of unemployment relief work, and it is a principle upon which I think everyone in this house is agreed. If the minister would only pledge himself to do that, he would get far greater support from this side of the house.

May I say this also-and I think it is very interesting in view of the splendid explanation given by the Minister of Marine in regard to the architects: my hon. friend will remember that last year I made a complaint, and made it again last night, with regard to the great number of departments involved in this work and the comparative absence of responsibility in connection with these various works. I was interested in a report appearing in the Ottawa 92582-179
Citizen to-day; I was reminded of it when I heard the explanation of the Minister of Marine with regard to architects and engineers. This is a summary of the report of the civil service commission, and the heading is:
Civil Service Commission Criticizes Government Policy Sharply . Points to Undesirable Effect of Ban Placed On Permanent Appointments and Promotions
This is a long report; I will read just this:
Likewise the commission is critical of the government's actions in placing outside the commission's jurisdiction the staffs of new Dublic bodies being set up, for example, staffs employed under the Natural Products Marketing Act and the Public Works Construction Act of 1934.
That is the report of the civil service commission with regard to the iniquitous effects of the system that is bound to grow up under a program of this kind, of engaging architects and engineers here and there and paying them apparently whatever salaries those gentlemen consider they should get, and what the ministers consider they should be paid.
I think the Minister of Railways and Canals should give us some details with regard to the railway grade crossings, as to the way in which this work is to be done. For a number of years I have -been urging that one of the best ways to utilize money for unemployment relief would be to eliminate a number of the level crossings that exist throughout the country and that have caused a great deal of trouble and many fatalities in recent years. I think we should have some idea as to how that work is to be done. I think it desirable that to a very large extent it should be done in the rural sections, because what has been done already has given better protection in the urban areas. In a time of great difficulty for the people living in the rural sections it would afford employment and a certain amount of relief, and I think we should have those details.
I should like to say a word with regard to these geological surveys, which have been dealt with so well by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre. Surely the Minister of Mines does not expect this house to pass this item without knowing where and how this money is to be expended.
There is another protest I want to make at this time. A night or two ago, I think, the minister said this Public Works Construction Act was passed on June 30. My recollection is that it was passed just before the house closed; it was introduced only a couple of days before. With a program of this kind is it fair to ask the house, when we expect to

Public Works Program

adjourn within a day or two, either to hold up the adjournment or to adopt the program without knowing all the details? Now that the acting Prime Minister and these various ministers are present I want to ask the government if they think the members of this houSe can discharge their responsibilities to their electors and at the same time allow this schedule to go through by six o'clock tomorrow evening. Is that a reasonable proposition, with this large expenditure? Is it a fact that this measure has been delayed while we talked about the tourist traffic and various other matters that do not mean a thing to the people of this country-including the budget debate conducted by the other side-until this time, with the idea that it might be put through without the members of this committee knowing exactly what it meant? That happened last year, and we thought we were being rather imposed upon then, when we had 185 items covering the public works construction program. It is true that a number of those items dealt with large amounts with which they should not have dealt. It is true that extracted from some of those large amounts, as I mentioned last night, were sums to build wharves, breakwaters and other things that should have been submitted to the committee in a separate list. Under this program almost anything can be done unless these sums are allocated. What I say, and I take full responsibility for it, is that these items should not pass this committee until we get details reasonably similar to those furnished last year. Do the government think that is an unfair request? Last year if it was intended to construct a little building costing 86,300-and some buildings cost much less-it was considered advisable to tell the committee where that building was to be constructed and what was the need for it. Do this government think they have increased in popularity and in the confidence of the people to the extent that this year they can get away with a thing like this? They know better than that.
I repeat, Mr. Chairman, that the members of this committee will not be discharging their full responsibility by allowing this bill to be put through in this way. So far as I am concerned, and I think this is the general view of the committee, unless we get details somewhat similar to those that have been given in connection with public works until this year, ever since we have had a public works department, I say this schedule should not pass.
fMr. Elliott.]

May I point out just how unreasonable in its present position the government really is. Let us turn to the main estimates as they were presented to this parliament and see what the government proposes for the geological survey. We find at page 47 of the main estimates for the fiscal year 1935-36, what the government is asking for as this year's appropriation for geological surveys. These are the words:
For explorations, surveys, and investigations; for publication of English and French editions of reports, maps, illustrations, etc., relating thereto; and for salaries and wages of explorers, topographers and others, $190,060.
According to the estimates, that is an increase of $8,750 over what was asked for in the previous year. Let us now turn to the schedule in the bill. Item two of the schedule is as follows:
Geological surveys and investigations in the Northwest Territories and elsewhere in Canada, $1,000,000.
The words "in the northwest territories and elsewhere in Canada" might as well be stricken out, because they are embraced in the general item for geological surveys and investigations. What is the position? We have in the main estimates, placed before parliament in the present year, an appropriation of $190,000 only, for the expenditure of which the government must give a full explanation; and we have in this one item in the schedule an amount of $1,000,000 for exactly the same services. Last year we had exactly the same situation to face. A little earlier in the session the government attempted to bring in its request for additional supply for relief purposes in the form of lump sums. Well, the government found it possible to give us the details. We are just as anxious as hon. gentlemen opposite to make provision for all that is necessary in the way of providing employment and unemployment relief, and I would suggest that, between now and the time we meet to-morrow afternoon, the several ministers who are asking for appropriations under this particular schedule get together the details they know will be expected and have them ready to give the house when we take up this measure again. As has been pointed out, this schedule is really a supplementary estimate affecting six different departments of the government. In respect to some of them, it not only duplicates but actually increases the moneys voted in the main estimates. In the case of the geological survey, for example, the amount is increased five times.

speechtext: May I say to my right hon. friend that whether or not it is wise to have a prolonged adjournment, the fact is that we have carried the motion for adjournment, which will mean that automatically this house adjourns tomorrow evening at six o'clock. That matter having been determined, I respectfully submit that it is idle to discuss the question now of continuing so far as this bill is concerned and not having an adjournment. But I can assure my right hon. friend that there is no desire so far as the government is concerned to deny the fullest information to the opposition if they will only permit the ministers to make reply with respect to the several items. If the house is agreeable I should be quite content by unanimous consent, if it is so desired, that we adjourn until eleven o'clock to-morrow morning, which would give us two extra hours for the purpose of securing full information on this bill. We desire to get royal assent to-morrow afternoon. This suggestion that we meet at eleven o'clock to-morrow may not meet the views of the house. It could be done only by unanimous consent, but I submit it in good faith and with the object of accommodating the house in getting the information it desires.

These have not been made; that is the point. Hon. gentlemen will be entitled next year to information with respect to expenditures made under this vote, but
they can get full details when the ordinary estimates are under consideration and when the supplementary estimates for this year are brought down. So that they are not denied information. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, to test the house, I move that when this house adjourns it shall stand adjourned until to-morrow at eleven o'clock. That motion can be entertained only by unanimous consent.

Speaking about following procedure that is customary and proper, I hope the government will be prepared to adopt, regarding these particular estimates affecting public works, the procedure followed with respect to public works generally, of having public tenders called for where the amount to be expended is in excess of 85,000.
